planting.note: Plant corms 3 inches deep in fall in very well-drained, sandy soil in full sun; rat's tail babiana needs a dry summer dormancy like other babianas and is best suited to zones 9-10 with Mediterranean-type winters.

directions: Rat's tail babiana is one of the most unusual bulbs in the Cape flora: the flowering stem bends sharply near its base so that a long, leafless, sterile extension trails along the ground while the upright fertile portion carries a dense spike of vivid red to purple-red flowers just above the fan of pleated leaves. That prostrate 'tail' is not decorative filler but a functional perch -- sunbirds land on it to feed from the tubular flowers, making this species a classic example of bird pollination in the iris family. Plant corms in fall in gritty, sharply drained soil in full sun, and expect the same fall-to-spring growing cycle and summer dormancy as other babianas. Because the trailing bract is part of the display, give plants an unobstructed spot in a rock garden or raised bed rather than crowding them among taller neighbors.

common_name: Venus Corn Lily (Rose-Pink Dark-Eyed Ixia Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in zones 8-10 in well-drained, sandy, slightly acid soil in full sun; in colder zones plant in spring after last frost and lift after foliage dies. Ixia requires a warm, dry summer dormancy to bloom well.

directions: Venus is a long-cultivated Dutch corn lily hybrid bearing clear rose-pink, star-shaped flowers centered on a small, sharply contrasting dark eye, carried in loose spikes on wiry stems above narrow, grasslike foliage. Like other Ixia hybrids the blooms stay tightly shut on overcast days and open fully only under strong sun, so reserve the brightest spot available and plant corms in bold drifts of 25 or more rather than singly. Let the foliage yellow and collapse completely after flowering before cutting it back, and in humid Gulf Coast summers lift the corms and store them dry until fall to prevent rot during the required dormant period.

common_name: Hogarth Corn Lily (Golden-Yellow Red-Eyed Ixia Hybrid)

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in zones 8-10 in well-drained, sandy, slightly acid soil in full sun; in colder zones plant in spring after last frost and lift after foliage dies. Ixia requires a warm, dry summer dormancy to bloom well.

directions: Hogarth is a historic Dutch-raised corn lily hybrid prized for its clear golden-yellow flowers, each marked at the base with a small ring of deep maroon-red that sharpens the contrast typical of Ixia hybrids. The wiry flower stems rise above narrow, sword-shaped leaves in late spring and, as with all corn lilies, the blooms close during overcast weather and open only in direct sun, so plant it in the sunniest corner of the garden. Massed in generous drifts it makes a long-lasting cut flower and combines well with the pinks of 'Rose Queen' and 'Mabel' for a mixed spring bulb display. Allow the foliage to die back naturally after bloom and, where summers are wet, lift and dry-store the corms to protect them through their required summer dormancy.

planting.note: Plant corms 2-3 inches deep in fall in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun; this Western Cape fynbos species grows through the cool, wet winter and needs to be kept nearly dry through its summer dormancy.

directions: Watsonia densiflora is a Western Cape fynbos species named for its tightly packed flower spikes, which carry an unusually dense cluster of pink to purplish-pink, funnel-shaped blooms compared with the more loosely spaced flowers of many other watsonias. It grows through the cool, wet winter months on mountain slopes and seeps, flowering in late spring before going summer-dormant, so watering should follow that same winter-wet, summer-dry rhythm in cultivation. Plant corms in gritty, well-drained soil in full sun, and treat it as a specialty bulb for raised beds or containers where its winter-growing cycle can be managed more easily than in a mixed summer border. Established clumps slowly increase by offsets but resent being disturbed too often.

common_name: Perfecta Rodgersia (Deep Pink Bronze-Leaved Hybrid Rodgersia)

planting.note: Plant divisions or container stock in spring in consistently moist, humus-rich soil in partial shade; 'Perfecta' is an old Arends-raised hybrid between R. aesculifolia and R. pinnata combining bronze-tinted foliage with unusually large, deep pink flower plumes.

directions: 'Perfecta' is a classic early-20th-century hybrid raised by the German nurseryman Georg Arends by crossing Rodgersia aesculifolia and Rodgersia pinnata, combining the bronze-flushed, horse-chestnut-like foliage of the former parent with the more richly colored plumes of the latter. In early summer it sends up tall, branching spikes of deep rosy-pink flowers well above a handsome mound of dark, bronze-tinted, palmately divided leaves that hold their color better through the season than many pinnata cultivars. It has held a place in shade and bog gardens for decades and has been recognized by the Royal Horticultural Society for its reliable performance in permanently moist soil. Give it rich, evenly moist to wet soil in partial shade or morning sun, sheltered from strong wind that can tatter the large leaves.

planting.note: Plant divisions or container starts in spring into consistently moist, humus-rich, slightly acidic woodland soil in partial to full shade; set crowns at soil level and mulch with leaf litter, as with its close relative P. tellimoides, though P. watanabei stays slightly more compact and flowers later in summer.

directions: Peltoboykinia watanabei is the smaller, later-flowering companion species to P. tellimoides, forming neat clumps of rounded, shallowly lobed, peltate leaves that emerge with a bronze flush before turning deep green through summer. In mid-to-late summer, wiry stems carry loose clusters of small, pale-yellow, bell-shaped flowers well above the foliage, several weeks after tellimoides has typically finished blooming. Its slightly more compact habit suits smaller shade gardens or the front of a woodland border where the bold, textural leaves can be appreciated up close. Keep the soil consistently moist and enrich yearly with leaf mold or compost, since like other peltoboykinias it will scorch and wilt quickly if allowed to dry out.

planting.note: Plant corms 3 inches deep in well-drained, fertile soil in fall; aethiopica cornflag is smaller and less aggressively spreading than the more commonly grown C. floribunda, making it a better choice for smaller gardens or contained plantings.

directions: Chasmanthe aethiopica is the smaller-growing of the two commonly cultivated cornflags, forming compact fans of pleated, sword-shaped leaves and, in late winter, arching spikes of tubular orange-red flowers held in two neat ranks along the stem. It shares the winter-growing, summer-dormant Cape bulb cycle and hummingbird- and sunbird-attracting flowers of C. floribunda but multiplies less rapidly by cormlets, so it stays better behaved in beds and borders rather than needing an area set aside for naturalizing. Plant corms in fall in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun to light shade, and withhold water through its summer dormancy. Its more restrained scale and spread make it the better choice for containers or foundation plantings where the larger C. floribunda would quickly overrun its neighbors.
sources: Kew Plants of the World Online

common_name: Dwarf Angel's Fishing Rod (Drakensberg Wand Flower)

planting.note: Divide established corms carefully in late spring when just barely in growth, or set out container-grown plants in humus-rich, well-drained but consistently moist soil in full sun; this dwarf, fast-maturing dierama flowers from seed within 2-3 years, sooner than most other wandflower species.

directions: Dierama dracomontanum is the compact, fast-maturing counterpart to the larger angel's fishing rods, native to high-elevation Drakensberg grasslands where it forms tufts of narrow, grasslike leaves and slender, arching stems only 2-3 feet tall. In summer it produces the same pendant, bell-shaped flowers as its larger relatives, typically in shades of pink, coral, or deep rose, dangling from thread-fine, wiry stems that sway gracefully in the wind. Because it comes into bloom from seed in as little as two to three years -- much sooner than the taller D. pulcherrimum -- it is the species most often recommended for gardeners wanting quicker results. Give it deep, humus-rich soil that stays evenly moist through summer, and avoid disturbing established clumps, since like all dieramas it resents transplanting once settled.
